The Lighthouse Keepers of Capo Rosso

By Giulia Marino

For more than a century the lighthouse at Capo Rosso was kept by the same two families, who took turns climbing its hundred and twelve steps every evening at dusk to light the lamp and every morning at dawn to put it out again, in every season and in every kind of weather.

The keepers kept a logbook, and the logbook survives. It records storms and calms, ships that passed and ships that did not, the price of lamp oil and the arrival of the first electric bulb in 1931, which one keeper described as "a small sun that needs no feeding and therefore no friend."

Life at the cape was quiet but never idle. Besides the lamp there were the lenses to polish, the clockwork to wind, the garden to tend and the children to teach, since the nearest school was a day's walk away along a path that the winter rains often washed into the sea.

When the light was finally automated in 1974 the last keeper, Rosa Bellini, wrote a single line in the logbook before handing over the keys: "The lamp will burn without us now, but it will not know why it burns." Read more in our archive or this link.

Today the keepers' house is a small museum, and the logbook lies open in a glass case at the foot of the stairs, turned each morning to the same date a hundred years before, so that visitors can read what the weather was like on their day, long ago, at the edge of the sea.
